articles.title: A member of one body

claims.t: Everything that reasons shares one reason, as limbs share one body, citizens one city, and every lit place one sun.
claims.shared: Four pictures (body, city, sunlight, soul) with one structure: a single thing present in many, and not split by being shared.

support.quote: The relation that the limbs of the body have in things that are united is the relation that rational beings have in things that stand apart
gives: as limbs share one body
Everything that reasons
support.follows: Rational beings, who stand apart, have the same relation to one another that the limbs of one body have.

support.quote: we are citizens. If that is so, we share in some civic body. If that is so, the universe is, as it were, a city.
gives: citizens one city
support.note: The last step of a chain that starts from mind and reason being common to us.
support.follows: We are citizens, we share in a civic body, and the universe is like a city.

support.quote: you yourself help to complete a civic whole
gives: citizens one city
support.note: Casaubon wrote that I was “made for” a common society. The Greek has no making here: one word says that I am one of the things that make the civic whole complete.
support.follows: I am one of those who make a civic whole complete.

support.quote: One light of the sun, even if it is divided by walls, by mountains
gives: every lit place one sun
support.follows: The light of the sun is one, even where walls and mountains divide it.

support.quote: One soul that has mind, even if it seems to be separated.
gives: shares one reason
support.follows: There is one soul that has mind, even though it seems to be separated.

support.quote: one soul that has mind has been portioned out among the rational ones
gives: shares one reason
Everything that reasons
support.follows: The beings that reason share one soul, the soul that has mind.

claims.changed: Marcus says “one soul that has mind” in 12.23 and 9.7, and “mind” and “reason” in 4.4. The fused claim says “reason” throughout.

claims.t: We are made for one another and for one common work, and that shared life is our own good.
claims.shared: Each says that a rational being is directed toward its own kind, whether by what it was built or born for (7.10, 5.15) or by the nature it shares in (9.7). 5.15 and 9.7 both say the direction is toward one another, and 5.15 and 7.10 both call it its own good.

support.quote: being built to do some one work together
gives: for one common work
We are made
support.follows: Rational beings are built to do one work together.

support.quote: everything that shares in a common nature of mind hurries toward its kin in the same way, or even more
gives: for one another
support.follows: Whatever shares in the common nature of mind hurries toward its own kin.

support.quote: therefore the good of a rational animal is community
gives: that shared life is our own good
support.follows: Living with others is what is good for a reasoning being.

support.quote: For that we were born for community has long since been shown.
gives: We are made
support.follows: It has long been shown that we were born for community.

support.quote: the worse things are for the sake of the better, and the better for the sake of one another? And things with a soul are better than things without one, and rational things better than things with a soul.
gives: for one another
support.note: Asked as a question that expects the answer yes: the better things are for the sake of one another. Marcus then ranks rational things highest.
support.follows: The better things are for the sake of one another, and rational things rank above everything else that has a soul.

support.quote: doing good does not yet delight you fully; you still do it as no more than the proper thing, not yet as doing good to yourself
gives: our own good
support.note: Marcus’s word for “doing good” means doing a kindness to someone else. The good of the other and my own are the same act.
support.follows: Doing good is also doing good to myself, and I have not grasped that while I do it only because it is proper.

claims.t: So each thing I do should aim at the common good, directly or at a distance, and holding to that one aim is what makes me one person.
claims.shared: Two passages set the same aim for what I do: 9.21 calls it “the social goal”, 11.19 “the social and civic one”. 11.19 adds what the single aim does for the one who holds it: that person is always the same. 9.21 gives the reverse case: an action without that reference “tears your life apart and does not let it be one”.

support.quote: so too let every action of yours help to complete a civic life
gives: each thing I do should
support.follows: Every action of mine should help to complete a civic life.

support.quote: any action of yours that does not refer, whether directly or at a distance, to the social goal tears your life apart and does not let it be one
gives: directly or at a distance
aim at the common good
support.follows: An action with no reference to the social goal, not even a distant one, tears my life apart and keeps it from being one.

support.quote: so too the aim to be set up must be the social and civic one
gives: aim at the common good
support.note: In the same sentence Marcus compares this aim to “the common goods”, the only goods that people judge alike.
support.follows: The aim I set up should be the social and civic one.

support.quote: whoever directs all their private impulses toward this aim will make all their actions alike, and in this way will always be the same
gives: holding to that one aim is what makes me one person
support.follows: A person who directs every private impulse toward this aim makes all their actions alike, and so is always the same.

claims.t: When I hate someone, wrong them, or resent what happens, I cut myself off, and not from that one thing only but from the whole.
claims.shared: Three pictures of severing (a branch, a limb, a seditious citizen). In each the person does it to himself, and in each the cut is from the whole.

support.quote: it is the human being who separates themselves from their neighbour, by coming to hate and turning away
gives: When I hate someone
I cut myself off
support.follows: A person separates themselves from a neighbour by coming to hate and turning away.

support.quote: they do not know that they have at the same time cut themselves away from the whole civic body as well
gives: from the whole
support.follows: In the same act, and without knowing it, he separates himself from the whole body of people.

support.quote: If you have ever seen a hand cut off, or a foot, or a severed head, lying somewhere or other apart from the rest of the body: that is what a person makes of themselves, as far as it is in their power, when they do not want what happens
gives: resent what happens
support.note: 8.32 counts not wanting what happens as a cut too.
support.follows: A person who does not want what happens makes of themselves, as far as they can, something like a hand or foot cut off from the body.

support.quote: or when they do something unsocial
gives: wrong them
support.follows: Doing something unsocial is counted as the same kind of act.

support.quote: he put it in the human being’s power not to be broken off from the whole in the first place
gives: I cut myself off
from the whole
support.follows: It is in a person’s own power not to be broken off from the whole.

support.quote: like the person in a citizen body who, for their own part, stands apart from such harmony
gives: I cut myself off
support.follows: It is like a person in a body of citizens who, for their own part, stands apart from its harmony.

claims.t: Having cut myself off, I can grow back into the whole, because nature is stronger than my leaving.
claims.shared: Two passages say the return is possible in almost the same words. 9.7 says something else: those who run away are overtaken all the same, because nature prevails. Joining the two with “because” is the editor’s step.

support.quote: we are allowed to grow together again with the one next to us and again to help to complete the whole
gives: I can grow back into the whole
support.follows: We are allowed to grow together again with the person next to us, and again to help make the whole complete.

support.quote: for one who has been broken off, he made it possible to come back again and grow together
gives: I can grow back
support.follows: A person who has been broken off has been given the power to come back and grow together again.

support.quote: though they run away, they are overtaken and hemmed in all the same; for nature prevails
gives: nature is stronger than my leaving
support.follows: Those who run away are overtaken all the same, because nature prevails.

claims.changed: 11.7 credits the return to Zeus and 8.32 to god. The fused claim credits nature, following 9.7.

inferences.why: No passage gives this reason: 11.7 credits the return to Zeus and 8.32 to god, and 9.7 speaks of people who run away and are overtaken, not of a return.

single.label: A practice
single.t: I shall often say to myself: I am a member, and not merely a part.
single.quote: you often say to yourself: “I am a limb [melos] of the whole made up of rational beings.”
single.why: Only 7.10 gives an exercise. It is kept as the article’s practice.
single.follows: I should often tell myself that I am a limb of the whole that rational beings make up.

single.label: A warning
single.t: The more often I cut myself off, the harder the return.
single.quote: when this kind of division happens many times, it makes what withdraws hard to unite and hard to restore
single.why: Only 11.7 says the return gets harder. One witness, so it is not fused into claim 5.
single.follows: When this division happens many times, what withdraws becomes hard to unite and hard to restore.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek instead of Casaubon. Passage numbers stay Casaubon’s. In modern editions 9.7 is 9.8 and 9.9, 5.15 is 5.16, 8.32 is 8.34, 7.10 is 7.13, 9.21 is 9.23, 12.23 is 12.30, 11.19 is 11.21, 8.52 is 8.54 and 11.7 is the first part of 11.8; 4.4 is the same.

Follows the Greek where Casaubon added to it. 9.21 does not say that I was “made for” a common society; it says that I help to complete a civic whole, so it no longer backs “We are made” in claim 2 and stands with the city picture of claim 1. 5.15 does not say that the best things “are made” for one another; it says that the better are for the sake of one another. 9.7 does not say that people “fly from nature”; it says that they run away and that nature prevails.
Reads body, city, sunlight and soul as four pictures of one claim. Marcus sets sunlight beside soul himself (12.23, 9.7); body and city he never lines up with them.
Joins the return (11.7, 8.32) to 9.7 with “because”. Marcus states the return and credits it to a god (Zeus in 11.7, “god” in 8.32); he does not derive it.
Says “nature” where two of the three passages behind claim 5 name a god: Zeus in 11.7, “god” in 8.32.
articles.limit: Nine of the ten passages feed the article. That is also a risk: fusing smooths over differences. 4.4 argues for the unity step by step, and 9.7 argues from the elements; the article states the unity and keeps neither argument. Ten of the 22 components of its claims rest on two or more passages; the other twelve are one passage’s words.

aside.8.52: A wish to think together with the mind that surrounds all things, as we breathe together with the air around us. Close to claim 1, but a wish and not a statement.

statement.t: I am a member of one body of reasoning beings, made for a shared life with them.

parts.words: made for a shared life with them

statement.kind: Many pictures, one claim; then its consequences
statement.form: The statement gathers claims 1 and 2. Claim 1 is fused from five passages that use four different pictures: body, city, sunlight, soul; claim 2 from three that say what we are made for. Claims 3 and 4 are what Marcus draws from it; the “because” of claim 5 is the editor’s.

empty.doubt: No passage in this section considers that reasoning beings might not be one. The doubt is taken up under Article 3.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, the two central claims gain a second author, the body picture gains an arch beside it, and the article gains a concrete act, a second exercise and a caution about crowds: I may step back from them, but I must not hate them. He disputes none of Marcus’s claims here.
seneca.statement: The statement stands. With Seneca it gains the arch: we do not only belong together, we hold one another up.

items.quote: we are the parts of one great body
gives: as limbs share one body
items.follows: We are all parts of one great body.
items.context: Seneca’s short rule for how to treat other people, given after the rule for worshipping the gods. “We” is gods and humans together: all that you see is one.

items.quote: Nature produced us related to one another, since she created us from the same source and to the same end. She engendered in us mutual affection, and made us prone to friendships.
gives: We are made
for one another
items.follows: Nature made us kin, from one source and for one end, and gave us affection for one another.
items.context: Seneca’s short rule for how to treat other people, given after the rule for worshipping the gods. “Us” is all human beings; “she” is Nature.

items.quote: no one can live happily who has regard to himself alone and transforms everything into a question of his own utility; you must live for your neighbour, if you would live for yourself
gives: that shared life is our own good
items.follows: No one lives happily for himself alone; to live for myself I have to live for another.
items.context: Opens on friendship (a friend’s interest is mine), then widens to all fellow men in 48.3. “Your neighbour” is any other person, the friend first.

items.label: why
items.t: We hold one another up as the stones of an arch do: without that support the arch falls.
items.why: Marcus has body, city, sunlight and soul. The arch adds something none of them states: that the whole stands only because its parts hold one another up.

support.quote: Our relations with one another are like a stone arch, which would collapse if the stones did not mutually support each other
support.follows: Human fellowship stands the way a stone arch does: only because its parts support one another.
support.context: Seneca’s short rule for how to treat other people, given after the rule for worshipping the gods. “Our relations with one another” is human fellowship as a whole, not one friendship.

items.label: action
items.t: My hands should be ready for anyone who needs help.
items.why: Marcus’s claim says to aim at the common good. Seneca names what that looks like when someone is in front of me.

support.quote: Through her orders, let our hands be ready for all that needs to be helped
support.follows: By Nature’s order we should be ready to help whatever needs help.
support.context: The practical close of Seneca’s short rule for how to treat other people. “Her” is Nature; those to be helped are people in need, like the shipwrecked and the starving just named.

items.label: practice
items.t: I shall keep one line in my heart and on my lips: I am human, and nothing human is foreign to me.
items.why: A second exercise beside Marcus’s own. The line is from the playwright Terence; Seneca quotes it as something to repeat.

support.quote: Let this verse be in your heart and on your lips: I am a man; and nothing in man’s lot Do I deem foreign to me.
support.follows: I should keep ready a line that says nothing human is foreign to me.
support.context: Seneca’s short rule for how to treat other people, given after the rule for worshipping the gods. “This verse” is a line of Terence, unnamed here, that Lucilius is told to keep ready.

items.label: breaks
items.t: I should not hate the many for being unlike me. I may withdraw into myself as far as I can, and keep the company that makes me better and that I can make better.
items.why: Marcus says that hating cuts me off. Seneca, writing about crowds that unsettle a character not yet firm, forbids the hatred and still advises stepping back. He does not speak of cutting off, so this is an addition, not a dispute.

support.quote: nor should you hate the many because they are unlike you. Withdraw into yourself, as far as you can. Associate with those who will make a better man of you. Welcome those whom you yourself can improve.
support.follows: I should not hate the crowd for being unlike me; I should withdraw into myself as far as I can and keep company that improves me and that I can improve.
support.context: A letter on avoiding crowds, which unsettle a character not yet firm. “The many” is the crowd, as at the games; “withdraw” is from it, not from everyone.

amend.t: , each of us holding the others up as the stones of an arch do

rejected.why: “we are his members”: members of God, in an argument that the soul is divine; not about one another
“parts and members of a single whole” are the virtues inside one soul
one soul, many virtues: a logic puzzle about virtue, not about people
an army or senate as a body of separate members: a preface to an argument about renown
the wise man’s good is common: his wisdom helps others too; an argument that he cannot be harmed
fellowship among men torn by avarice: a history of early mankind, not what I do
“this whole world is my country”: about travel and place, not fellow citizens
“born to love all men”: a premise in an argument about renown; 95.52 says it directly
nature draws men to each other: on friendship; 95.52 already says it
the wise man’s good stays within himself: a real limit on claim 2, proposed to the owner, not added
fellowship with all men helps friendship: continues 48.2, which is in use
reason as a portion of the divine spirit: argues that goods are equal, not that we share reason
our reason derives from divine reason: about the parts of the soul
the sun unimpaired by obstacles: a picture of virtue, not of one light shared
peace and liberty belong whole to each: thanks owed to rulers, not fellowship
wrongdoing poisons the doer: about ingratitude; self-harm, not being cut off
every animal looks out for itself first: describes instinct, gives no rule for action
grafting a vine: about a pupil too spoiled to take teaching, not a return to fellowship
avoid the many, the few, the one: solitude is safe only for the good; 7.8 is the fuller text
the unready are better in any company than alone: the reverse of 7.8, kept as a note on his consistency
he withdrew to write for later generations: confirms that his stepping back is no break with people

articles.title: The work that belongs to me

claims.t: Among other people, I mean well by my own kind and aim at social acts. This comes first.
claims.shared: All three lists have this item. 7.30 says it “comes first”. 8.25 puts it first in its list and 8.6 second, after judgment, and neither of them ranks it. Only 7.30 ranks it. Where the claim says “social acts”, 7.30 says only “being social”; the acts are 8.6’s word.

support.quote: So what comes first in the human make-up is being social.
gives: aim at social acts
This comes first
support.note: 7.30 ranks it: “what comes first”. It says “being social” and does not speak of acts; the sentence before it says that what each being has to do follows from its make-up.
support.follows: What comes first in the way a human being is made is being social.

support.quote: what is proper to a human being is goodwill towards their own kind
gives: mean well by my own kind
support.follows: It is proper to a human being to have goodwill towards their own kind.

support.quote: when it directs its impulses only to social acts
gives: aim at social acts
support.note: Second in the list of 8.6.
support.follows: A reasoning nature does well when it directs its impulses only to social acts.

support.quote: in so far as we must do good to them and bear with them
gives: mean well by my own kind
support.follows: We must do good to other people and bear with them.

claims.t: With my body, I do not let what it feels rule me. Reason should hold first place and not be overpowered by the senses and impulses: it is by nature fitted to make use of them.
claims.shared: Two of the three lists have the item about not yielding: 7.30 names “what the body undergoes” and 8.25 “the movements of the senses”. 8.6 has none about the body; it speaks of desires and aversions in general. That reason should hold first place over the senses and impulses, and is by nature fitted to make use of them, is said by 7.30 alone.

support.quote: Second is not giving way to what the body undergoes
gives: I do not let what it feels rule me
support.follows: A human being should not give way to what the body undergoes.

support.quote: looking down on the movements of the senses
gives: I do not let what it feels rule me
support.follows: It is proper to a human being to look down on the stirrings of the senses.

support.quote: the movement of mind wants to hold first place and not to be overpowered by them. And rightly so, for it is by nature fitted to make use of all of those.
gives: Reason should hold first place
not be overpowered by the senses and impulses: it is by nature fitted to make use of them
support.follows: The mind rightly wants to come first and not be overpowered by the senses and impulses, because by nature it is fitted to make use of them.
support.note: “Them” and “those” are the movement of the senses and the movement of impulse, named in the sentence before.

support.quote: but I do see one that rises up against pleasure: self-control
support.note: Names the virtue that does this work.
support.follows: Self-restraint is the virtue that resists pleasure.
gives: I do not let what it feels rule me

claims.t: In my judgments I take care: I do not accept what is false or uncertain, and I do not judge in a hurry.
claims.shared: All three lists have this item. 8.6 puts it first and 7.30 last.

support.quote: Third in the rational make-up is not being hasty and not being deceived.
gives: I do not judge in a hurry
I do not accept what is false or uncertain
support.follows: A human being should avoid haste in judging and should not be deceived.

support.quote: a rational nature’s road goes well when, among its impressions, it assents to nothing false and nothing unclear
gives: I do not accept what is false or uncertain
support.follows: A reasoning nature does well when it does not agree to anything false or unclear.

support.quote: telling the persuasive impressions apart
gives: I take care
support.follows: It is proper to a human being to tell persuasive impressions apart.

support.quote: what is just will not be kept if we either care about the things in between, or are easily deceived, hasty and changeable
gives: I do not judge in a hurry
I do not accept what is false or uncertain
support.note: Not from a list of what is proper to man: said of what destroys justice.
support.follows: What is just cannot be kept by people who care about the things in between, or who are easily deceived, hasty and changeable.

claims.t: Doing this work is living according to my own nature. So long as I am doing it, pain is not against nature for me, and so it is not bad for me. And doing it makes me content.
claims.shared: Joy and being content are two words in two passages for one thing: doing my proper work is its own reward. Only 7.8 says that an action in accordance with reason is in accordance with nature. Only 6.31 speaks of pain: so long as I am doing a human being’s work it is not against nature for me, and so it is not bad for me.

support.quote: A human being’s joy is to do what is proper to a human being.
gives: doing it makes me content
support.follows: A human being’s joy is in doing what is proper to a human being.

support.quote: Every nature is content with itself when its road goes well.
gives: doing it makes me content
support.follows: Every nature is content with itself when its course goes well.

support.quote: So too for a human being, as a human being, pain is not against nature, so long as they are doing a human being’s work.
gives: So long as I am doing it, pain is not against nature for me
support.follows: For a human being who is doing a human being’s work, pain is not against nature.

support.quote: And if it is not against nature for them, it is not bad for them either.
gives: and so it is not bad for me
support.follows: If pain is not against nature for a person, it is not bad for that person either.

support.quote: For the rational animal, the same action is in accordance with nature and in accordance with reason.
support.note: Why work done by reason counts as natural.
support.follows: For a reasoning being, acting by reason and acting by nature are the same.
gives: living according to my own nature

claims.t: The work is the act itself, not what happens to me. And when something blocks one action, dealing with that obstacle becomes my next action.
claims.shared: Two passages place the work in the acting itself; only 9.14 rules out what happens to me. Three more, in three images, say an obstacle is turned into what I work on next: 5.17 says the mind shifts it “into what comes first”; 4.1 and 8.33 say it is made “into material for itself”.

support.quote: Reason and the art of reasoning are powers that are content with themselves and with the works that are their own.
gives: The work is the act itself
support.follows: Reason needs nothing beyond itself and its own activity.

support.quote: The bad and the good of the rational and civic animal lie not in what it undergoes but in what it does
gives: The work is the act itself
not what happens to me
support.follows: The good and the bad of a rational, civic animal lie in what it does, not in what happens to it.

support.quote: For the mind turns round every obstacle to its activity and shifts it into what comes first
gives: when something blocks one action, dealing with that obstacle becomes my next action
support.follows: The mind turns every obstacle to its activity around and makes it the thing that comes first.

support.quote: what is brought in instead it makes into material for itself
gives: when something blocks one action, dealing with that obstacle becomes my next action
support.follows: Whatever comes in place of what it was aiming at, the ruling part makes into material for itself.

support.quote: the rational animal can make every obstacle into material for itself and use it for whatever its impulse was set on
gives: when something blocks one action, dealing with that obstacle becomes my next action
support.follows: A reasoning being can use whatever obstacles it meets as material for what it set out to do.

single.label: Only in one list
single.t: I may add a fourth work: to contemplate the nature of the universe.
single.quote: contemplating the nature of the whole
single.why: Neither of the other two lists has it, so it is not fused. Article 4 takes it up.
single.follows: Contemplating the nature of the whole is also proper to a human being.

single.label: Only in one list
single.t: And I may welcome gladly whatever the common nature deals out.
single.quote: when it welcomes everything allotted by the common nature
single.why: Only 8.6 puts this in the list. It is the whole subject of Article 3.
single.follows: A reasoning nature does well when it welcomes everything the common nature allots.

single.label: A direction
single.t: To these I shall apply my mind and go straight on.
single.quote: So let the ruling part hold to these and carry its straight road through
single.why: Only 7.30 turns the list into an instruction.
single.follows: The ruling part should hold to these three things and go straight on to the end.

single.label: What I then have
single.t: When I hold to these, my mind has all that belongs to it.
single.quote: and it has what is its own
single.why: Only 7.30 says this, and it names no feeling. Casaubon wrote “her end, and by consequent her happiness”, so the article used to count it with joy and content in the claim about being content. The Greek says only that the ruling part “has what is its own”.
single.follows: A ruling part that holds to these three things has what is its own.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek instead of Casaubon. Passage numbers stay Casaubon’s. In modern editions 7.30 is 7.55, 8.25 is 8.26 and 8.27, 8.6 is 8.7, 5.17 is 5.20, 8.37 is 8.39, 11.9 is 11.10, 6.31 is 6.33 and 6.34, 7.8 is 7.11, 9.14 is 9.16 and 8.33 is 8.35; 5.14 is 5.14 and 5.15, and 4.1 is the same. Of the passages set aside, 11.18 is 11.20 and 7.42 is 7.72; 9.1 is the same.
Treats the three lists as versions of one list. Marcus never says they are the same list.

Names the three places “other people, my body, my judgments”, and sums them up as “letting reason lead”. The names and the summary are the editor’s: 7.30 says the movement of mind “wants to hold first place” over the movements of the senses and of impulse, and 7.8 that the same action is in accordance with nature and with reason; neither says it of other people or of judging.
Joins the passages that place the work in the act itself with those about obstacles in claim 5, as two sides of one point.

Follows the Greek where Casaubon said more, or something else. He wrote “the common good” where 7.30 says “being social” and 8.6 “social acts”; “lusts” and “appetites” where 7.30 speaks of “what the body undergoes” and 8.25 of “the movements of the senses”; “ordained to command all in the body” where 7.30 says “fitted to make use of all of those”; and “passion” where 9.14 says “what it undergoes”. The claims now say what the Greek says.

Withdraws three things the article said on Casaubon’s wording alone. That the work is not its result rested on his “final ends and consummations of actions” in 5.14; the Greek there speaks of things that do not fall to a human being as a human being, and says nothing of results. That proper work cannot harm me rested on his “labour” in 6.31; the translation from the Greek has “pain”, and claim 4 now says what Marcus says of pain. That the mind then has “her happiness” in 7.30 is his addition; the Greek says it “has what is its own”, and that line now stands alone under “said once”.
articles.limit: The alignment is clean for two of the three items. The item about the body is missing from 8.6, and each list has something the others lack. Those leftovers are shown under “said once”. Inside the claims, six things rest on one passage each: that being social comes first (7.30), that reason should hold first place over the senses and impulses (7.30), that I take care in judging (8.25), that this work is living according to my own nature (7.8), that pain met in it is not bad for me (6.31), and that the work is not what happens to me (9.14).

aside.11.18: The elements keep their place; the mind that resents does not. An argument for submission, nearer to Article 3.
aside.9.1: A long passage that calls injustice, lying and pleasure-seeking impious. It argues for the same three works from piety, a ground the article does not use.
aside.7.42: What the rational and civic power finds to be neither of mind nor social, it judges inferior to itself. A test for objects, not a description of the work.

statement.t: My work is to let reason lead in how I treat other people, in how I handle my body, and in how I judge.
statement.form: Three passages each give a list, in different words and at different lengths: 7.30 lists what comes first, second and third in the human make-up, 8.25 what is proper to a human being, and 8.6 the ways in which a rational nature’s road goes well. The statement and the three claims under “In action” come from aligning those lists item by item.

empty.doubt: No passage in this section asks what remains if reason is not what a human being is for.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, four of the five claims gain a second author, Practice gains a way to stay my own master amid business, and “When it breaks” gains what Marcus does not say in this section: to look to the reason for an action and not to its result. To the claim about the body he adds that it may still be indulged somewhat.
seneca.statement: The statement stands. Seneca names its ground outright: reason is what is peculiar to a human being.

items.quote: I am naturally born to love all men
gives: mean well by my own kind
items.follows: I am born to love all human beings.
items.context: Seneca argues that praise from good men is a good for the man praised; “I” is that good man, glad of it because he loves all people by nature.

items.quote: I do not maintain that the body is not to be indulged at all; but I maintain that we must not be slaves to it
gives: I do not let what it feels rule me
items.follows: The body may be indulged somewhat, but we must not be its slaves.
items.context: On our love of the body, which we must guard; “it” is the body, and the slavery he describes is living for it and fearing on its behalf.

items.quote: our alliance shall nevertheless not be one of equality; the soul shall bring all quarrels before its own tribunal
gives: Reason should hold first place
items.follows: While soul and body are joined they are not equals: the soul judges every dispute between them.
items.context: Seneca refuses to live as his body’s chattel; “our alliance” is the soul’s with the body while they are bound together. A resolve, not a law of nature.

items.quote: And what is it which this reason demands of him? The easiest thing in the world,—to live in accordance with his own nature
gives: living according to my own nature
items.follows: What reason asks of a human being is to live by his own nature.
items.context: Seneca has just said a man’s own good is reason perfected in the soul; “his own nature” is the nature of man as a reasoning animal.

items.quote: What then is peculiar to man? Reason. When this is right and has reached perfection, man’s felicity is complete.
gives: doing it makes me content
items.follows: Reason is what is peculiar to a human being; when it is right and perfected, his happiness is complete.
items.context: Each thing is judged by the good that is its own, as a stag by speed; “this” is reason, and he speaks of reason made perfect, not of work under way.

items.quote: Because of his poverty he is prevented from showing how the State should be handled; but he teaches, none the less, how poverty should be handled.
gives: when something blocks one action, dealing with that obstacle becomes my next action
items.follows: Kept by poverty from showing how a state should be handled, the wise man shows how poverty should be handled.
items.context: Seneca answers that hardship cannot stop the wise man as a storm stops a pilot; “he” is the wise man, whom poverty keeps out of public life.

items.label: practice
items.t: I lend myself to my affairs; I do not hand myself over to them.
items.why: Marcus says to hold to the three things and go straight on. Seneca, writing about keeping time for study, says how he stays his own master amid business.

support.quote: I do not surrender myself to my affairs, but loan myself to them
support.follows: I can take part in business without giving myself up to it.
support.context: Seneca denies that business keeps anyone from study; “my affairs” are his engagements, and what he keeps back is his time and his own thoughts.

items.label: breaks
items.t: I look to the reason for what I do, not to how it turns out. The beginning is in my power; fortune decides the outcome.
items.why: Marcus’s claim places the work in the act itself. Seneca adds that the wise man looks to the reason for an action and not to its result. The article once said this of Marcus too, on Casaubon’s wording of 5.14; the Greek there does not speak of results.

support.quote: the wise man regards the reason for all his actions, but not the results. The beginning is in our own power; fortune decides the issue
gives: I look to the reason for what I do, not to how it turns out
The beginning is in my power; fortune decides the outcome
support.follows: The wise man looks to the reasons for what he does, not to how it turns out: the start is ours, the outcome is fortune’s.
support.context: Seneca has admitted that a careful life cannot guarantee safety; “the results” are how the wise man’s actions turn out, which fortune decides.

articles.title: What happens to me

claims.role: It comes from one chain of causes
claims.t: What happens to me is not chance alone. All things are linked together, and it comes from a chain of causes, the same that produced me.
claims.shared: Five passages use one family of words: interwoven, interweaving, spun together, fit together, kinship. Two (7.6, 4.36) say that things hold together. Three (10.5, 5.8, 1.17) say that what happens comes through that holding. Only 10.5 says the same causes produced me, and only 1.17 speaks of chance. No passage has the word “chain”: it is the editor’s plain word for the interweaving of causes (10.5) and for what is spun together out of the oldest causes (5.8).

support.quote: Whatever happens to you was being made ready for you beforehand, from all time, and the interweaving of causes was spinning together, from eternity, both your existence and the happening of this.
gives: it comes from a chain of causes
the same that produced me
support.follows: The causes that produced me also produced everything that happens to me.

support.quote: it came about for you, and was ordered for you, and stood in some relation to you, spun together from far back out of the oldest causes
gives: it comes from a chain of causes
support.follows: What happens to me was spun together from far back, out of the oldest causes, and it came about for me.

support.quote: All things are interwoven with one another, and the bond is sacred
gives: All things are linked together
support.follows: Everything is connected to everything else.

support.quote: What comes from chance is not without nature, or without the spinning together and interweaving of the things that providence governs.
gives: is not chance alone
chain of causes
support.follows: Even what comes from chance is not apart from nature, or from the spinning together and interweaving of the things that providence governs.

support.quote: just as the things that exist have been arranged to fit together, so the things that come to be show not bare succession but a wonderful kinship
gives: All things are linked together
support.follows: The things that exist are arranged to fit together, and in the same way the things that happen do not merely follow one another: they are akin.

claims.changed: “Not a random blow from outside” is gone: no passage says “from outside”, and 4.36 sets its order against a bare succession, not against chance. 7.6 now backs “linked together”, which is what its “interwoven with one another” says, and no longer “chain of causes”, of which it says nothing. “Not chance” became “not chance alone” when the quotes moved to the project’s English: 1.17 does not deny chance, it says that what comes from chance is not without nature.

claims.t: It serves the whole of which I am a part. What serves the whole is good for every part, and a part must not complain of it.
claims.shared: Three passages say that what happens is good for the whole (6.40, 5.8) or comes about for its sake (9.38), and two that I am a part of it (1.17, 9.38). Two go on to the part, and each says a different thing: 1.17 that what the nature of the whole brings, and what preserves it, is good for every part; 9.38 that the part must not find fault. They share the subject, not the conclusion.

support.quote: Whatever happens to each is good for the whole.
gives: It serves the whole
support.follows: What happens to any individual is useful to the whole.

support.quote: it would not bring this to anyone if it did not bring good to the whole
gives: It serves the whole
support.follows: Nothing would be brought to anyone if it did not bring good to the whole.

support.quote: there is besides what is necessary, and what benefits the whole universe, of which you are a part
gives: of which I am a part
support.follows: There is also what is necessary and what benefits the whole universe, and I am a part of that universe.

support.quote: what the nature of the whole brings is good for every part of nature, and so is what preserves that nature
gives: What serves the whole is good for every part
support.follows: Whatever the nature of the whole brings, and whatever preserves that nature, is good for every part.

support.quote: everything happens, one thing upon another, as to one body, from one source that has mind, and the part must not find fault with what comes about for the sake of the whole
gives: of which I am a part
What serves the whole
a part must not complain of it
support.follows: If everything happens as to one body, from one source that has mind, the part must not find fault with what comes about for the sake of the whole.

claims.changed: Was “what serves the whole is not bad for the part”, a middle wording that neither passage says: 1.17 says “good”, and 9.38 speaks of finding fault, not of harm. Each now backs its own words. “Has no reason to complain” became “must not complain” when the quotes moved to the project’s English: 9.38 says the part “must not find fault”, and the Greek has nothing for the 1634 translation’s “against reason”.

claims.t: So I shall accept it, and more than accept it: fit myself to it and be glad of it, as I take a harsh prescription for the sake of health.
claims.shared: Four passages give the same instruction with rising warmth: accept, fit yourself, welcome, hold dear, love. Only 5.8 says “accept”; 5.8, 6.39 and 3.17 say “welcome”, which is more. Only 5.8 has Asclepius, the god of healing, and his orders. “So” is Marcus’s own step in 5.8 (“Let us accept these things, then”; “So you should hold dear what falls to you”). “And more than accept it” is the editor’s link and rests on no quote.

support.quote: Let us accept these things, then, as we accept the things Asclepius orders. After all, many of those too are rough, but we welcome them in the hope of health.
gives: as I take a harsh prescription for the sake of health
So I shall accept it
support.follows: I should accept what happens as I accept what Asclepius, the god of healing, orders: much of it is rough, and I welcome it in the hope of health.

support.quote: welcome everything that comes about, even if it seems rather harsh
gives: be glad of it
support.follows: I should welcome everything that comes about, even when it seems harsh.

support.quote: Fit yourself to the things your lot has joined you to
gives: fit myself to it
support.follows: I should adapt myself to the circumstances I have been given.

support.quote: to love and welcome the things that happen to them and are spun together for them
gives: be glad of it
support.follows: The stance named here is to love and welcome the things that happen to me and are spun together for me.
support.note: In 3.17 this is what is left as the good person’s own; that part of the sentence lies outside the quote.

support.quote: one must arrive pure, quiet, ready to be released, fitted to one’s own portion without being forced
gives: fit myself to it
support.follows: I must arrive pure, quiet and ready to be released, fitted to my own portion without being forced.
support.note: In 3.17 the place of arrival is the end of life; those words lie outside the quote.

support.quote: they certainly did deliberate about the affairs of the community, at least, and these things too, which happen as a consequence of those, I ought to welcome and hold dear
gives: be glad of it
support.follows: What happens as a consequence of what the gods deliberated for the community, I ought to welcome and hold dear.

claims.t: None of it is unusual. Sickness, death and slander are as ordinary as roses in spring.
claims.shared: Two passages make what happens familiar and recurring: 4.36 calls it ordinary and familiar, and 9.26 says the cycles of the universe are the same from age to age.

support.quote: Everything that happens is as ordinary and familiar as the rose in spring and fruit in summer.
gives: as ordinary as roses in spring
None of it is unusual
support.follows: Everything that happens is as ordinary as the seasons.

support.quote: illness is like that too, and death, and slander, and plotting
gives: Sickness, death and slander
support.follows: Illness, death, slander and plotting are ordinary in the same way.

support.quote: The cycles of the universe are the same, up and down, from age to age.
gives: None of it is unusual
support.follows: The cycles of the universe are the same in every age.

claims.t: And if nothing governs the world, I still have a reason of my own, and can govern what is mine with it.
claims.shared: Four passages grant the other case, that nothing governs. Three end with something left to me: an order not to act at random myself (9.26), a mind that rules, in myself (12.11), and freedom to deliberate about myself (6.39). Only 12.11 names that mind; the claim calls it reason. 9.38 ends only with “Why, then, are you troubled?”. This is the most repeated move in the section.

support.quote: if it is randomness, do not act at random yourself as well
gives: And if nothing governs the world
can govern what is mine
support.follows: Even if everything is randomness, I must not act at random myself.
support.note: Here Marcus gives only the order not to act at random myself. He does not name reason.

support.quote: if it is a jumble with nothing ruling it, be glad that in such a rough sea you yourself have in yourself a mind that rules
gives: And if nothing governs the world
I still have a reason of my own
can govern what is mine with it
support.follows: Even if the world is a jumble with nothing ruling it, I have in myself a mind that rules, and I can be glad of that.

support.quote: if in fact they deliberate about nothing that concerns us, then I am free to deliberate about myself
gives: And if nothing governs the world
can govern what is mine with it
support.follows: Even if the gods plan nothing, I may still deliberate about my own affairs.

support.quote: there are atoms, and nothing else but a stirred brew and a scattering. Why, then, are you troubled?
support.note: The question closes both cases, the one body and the atoms. On the atomist case Marcus does not say here that reason remains; he only asks why I am troubled.
support.follows: If there are only atoms, and nothing but a stirred brew and a scattering, there is nothing for me to be troubled about.
gives: And if nothing governs the world

single.label: A warning
single.t: Each time I am displeased with what happens, I cut through the connection of the whole, as far as lies in me.
single.quote: the complete whole is maimed if you cut through the connection and continuity at any point at all, of its causes just as of its parts. And you do cut through it, as far as it lies with you, whenever you are discontented, and in a way you destroy it.
single.why: One witness in this section. 8.32, in the section behind Article 1, makes a like point with a severed limb. The quote says only “whenever you are discontented”; that the discontent is with what happens comes from the sentence that opens this argument in 5.8, “you should hold dear what falls to you”, outside the quote.
single.follows: Each time I am discontented I cut through the connection of the whole, as far as it lies with me, and in a way I destroy it.

single.label: An addition
single.t: And I shall love the people fate has given me to live with, and love them truly.
single.quote: love the people your lot has put you among, but truly
single.why: Only 6.35 turns acceptance toward people. It is kept apart for a later article.
single.follows: I should truly love the people my lot has put me among.

decisions: Presents the section as one argument by cases. Marcus gives the cases in four passages and never the whole chain in one place.

Keeps apart the two things said about the part: 1.17 says that what the nature of the whole brings, and what preserves it, is good for every part; 9.38 says that the part must not find fault. An earlier draft merged them into “not bad for the part”, which neither says.

Records no editor’s inference. The one “so”, in the claim under In action, is Marcus’s own: 5.8 says “So you should hold dear what falls to you, for two reasons”. The reasons are that it was spun together for me out of the oldest causes, and that it is a cause of good progress for the one that governs the whole.
Says nothing about acting to change what can be changed. That is Article 2. Accepting what has happened is not an instruction to do nothing.
articles.limit: Claims 1 to 4 hold only in the first case. If you do not think the world is governed, the article reduces to claim 5, and Marcus would not object: he says so himself. That what serves the whole is good for me has one witness here (1.17); Article 6 returns to it from its own passages.

aside.7.22: A list of reminders about convention, death, pain and fame. Too many subjects to fuse with anything here.
aside.3.12: Questions to ask of any impression, tracing each thing to god, to the shared lot and chance, or to a kinsman. An exercise in examining impressions, nearer to judgment than to accepting what happens.
aside.4.8: What happens, happens justly. A stronger claim than claim 2, and only this passage makes it.

statement.t: Whatever happens to me, I accept it and do not complain.
statement.kind: An argument by cases, found four times
statement.form: This is an argument by cases, and Marcus makes it four times in this section. “Why” holds the first case, that the world is governed. “If I doubt it” holds the second. “Do not complain” gathers three wordings: find fault (9.38), be discontented (5.8), and be troubled (9.38), in a question that closes both cases.

empty.practice: No passage used in this article gives an exercise. Asclepius and his orders in 5.8 are a comparison, not something to do. 3.12, set aside, has one (to say of each thing where it comes from), but its subject is judging impressions.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca every claim gains a second author, the empty Practice label gets two exercises, “Why” gets a further argument, and “In action” gains what I may still prefer before a hardship comes. Nothing of Marcus’s is challenged.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement gains a preparation: I accept what happens, and I think ahead to it.

items.quote: Such affairs come by order, and not by accident.
gives: is not chance
items.follows: Troubles like these come by order, not by accident.
items.context: Seneca has just listed his own illness, sick slaves and lost income; “such affairs” are those troubles, which he calls inevitable.

items.quote: the very agencies which seem to bring harm are working for the preservation of the world
gives: It serves the whole
items.follows: What seems to harm me is working to preserve the world.
items.context: Seneca names the inner defence against Fortune: not chafing at what happens. “The very agencies” are the events that seem to harm us.

items.quote: I have trained myself not merely to obey God, but to agree with His decisions
gives: accept it, and more than accept it
items.follows: I can do more than obey what is decided: I can agree with it.
items.context: Said of the times “when everything seems to go hard”; “His decisions” are the illness and losses of 96.1, which Seneca says are decreed.

items.quote: It is to this law that our souls must adjust themselves, this they should follow, this they should obey. Whatever happens, assume that it was bound to happen, and do not be willing to rail at Nature.
gives: I shall accept it
fit myself to it
items.follows: My soul should adjust itself to nature’s law, take whatever happens as bound to happen, and not rail at it.
items.context: “This law” is nature’s order of changing seasons and opposites, which we cannot alter; “it” is whatever that order brings.

items.quote: None of these things is unusual or unexpected.
gives: None of it is unusual
items.follows: Setbacks like these are neither unusual nor unexpected.
items.context: “These things” are Lucilius’s slaves running away; Seneca widens it at once to every knock on life’s journey.

items.quote: whether Chance drives and tosses human affairs without method, philosophy ought to be our defence
gives: And if nothing governs the world
items.follows: Even if chance drives everything, philosophy is still my defence.
items.context: Seneca answers the objection that philosophy is useless if fate, God or chance rules: in each case we need it. “Chance” is the third case.

items.label: why
items.t: And refusing does not spare me: fate leads the willing and drags the unwilling.
items.why: Marcus argues from the good of the whole. This argues that I go either way. Marcus only touches it, in 12.11 (“why do you strain against it?”), which this article uses for something else. Seneca gives the line as Cleanthes’s, in his own Latin.

support.quote: the willing soul Fate leads, but the unwilling drags along
support.follows: Fate takes me along whether I am willing or not.
support.context: The last line of Cleanthes’s prayer to Jupiter, which Seneca puts into Latin to close a letter on following nature’s law; the soul is anyone’s.
gives: fate leads the willing and drags the unwilling

items.label: practice
items.t: I shall think ahead to everything that can happen, not only to what usually does, so that the blow is lighter when it comes.
items.why: The passages used here give no exercise. Seneca gives this one in three letters. He also warns against overdoing it: in Ep. 13.10 he says not to run out to meet a suffering that has not come.

support.quote: Our minds should be sent forward in advance to meet all problems, and we should consider, not what is wont to happen, but what can happen.
support.follows: I should think ahead to what can happen, not only to what usually happens.
gives: think ahead to everything that can happen, not only to what usually does
support.context: Written after fire destroyed Lyons and shook his friend Liberalis; “all problems” are whatever Fortune can do, since the unexpected weighs heaviest.

support.quote: If an evil has been pondered beforehand, the blow is gentle when it comes.
support.follows: A misfortune I have already thought about hits less hard.
gives: the blow is lighter when it comes
support.context: Follows a picture of the man who hears of chains and exile calmly; “an evil” is any such threatened hardship, new only to the unprepared.

support.quote: That which has been long expected comes more gently.
support.follows: What I have long expected is easier when it arrives.
gives: the blow is lighter when it comes
support.context: The closing advice of a letter on illness: keep Fortune’s whole power before your eyes. “That which” is any blow she may strike.

items.label: practice
items.t: For a set number of days I shall live on the plainest food and clothing, and ask myself: is this what I was afraid of?
items.why: A second exercise, done with the body and not only in thought. It rehearses a loss before it comes; that is how it bears on accepting what happens.

support.quote: Set aside a certain number of days, during which you shall be content with the scantiest and cheapest fare, with coarse and rough dress, saying to yourself the while: “Is this the condition that I feared?”
support.follows: I should spend set days living poorly and ask myself whether this is what I feared.
support.context: A lesson for the Saturnalia: rehearse poverty while Fortune is kind, so that she cannot catch me off guard. “The condition” is being poor.

items.label: doubt
items.t: In that case my stance changes too: a god I follow gladly, but chance I endure, and defy.
items.why: Marcus says only that I can still govern myself. Seneca adds how to stand toward a world run by chance.

support.quote: She will encourage us to obey God cheerfully, but Fortune defiantly; she will teach us to follow God and endure Chance.
support.follows: Philosophy teaches me to obey a god cheerfully, and to endure chance and defy it.
support.context: “She” is philosophy, our defence whether fate, God or chance rules; the sentence sets how to stand toward God against how to stand toward Fortune.

items.label: action
items.t: I need not wish for the hardship. I may prefer to be spared it; what I want, if it must be borne, is to bear it with courage.
items.why: Marcus says to be glad of what comes; he does not say what I may wish beforehand. Seneca does. It is not a disagreement: Seneca too is pleased with what has come (Ep. 96.2, 74.20).

support.quote: I should prefer to be free from torture; but if the time comes when it must be endured, I shall desire that I may conduct myself therein with bravery, honour, and courage.
gives: I may prefer to be spared it; what I want, if it must be borne, is to bear it with courage
support.follows: I may prefer not to be tortured; if it must be endured, what I desire is to bear it with courage.
support.context: Lucilius asked whether brave endurance of torture is a thing to pray for; Seneca answers that the bravery is desirable, not the torture.

support.quote: The conclusion is, not that hardships are desirable, but that virtue is desirable, which enables us patiently to endure hardships.
gives: I need not wish for the hardship
support.follows: Hardships are not what is desirable; the virtue that lets me endure them is.
support.context: The conclusion Seneca draws from torture, war and illness; “virtue” is brave conduct in them, the only thing there he calls desirable.

welcomes hardship only as the price of a duty; a different condition
willing what necessity forces, said of dying only
consolation for a death; about mortality, not whatever happens

articles.title: The reason that governs the whole

claims.t: The world is one thing, ordered throughout, and all things in it are bound to one another.
claims.shared: Three passages call the world one (“one living thing”, “unity”, “the one and entire thing”), two call it ordered, and two say that all things in it are tied together. 6.8 puts order as one of two cases; 4.22 names two cases and then decides: “But in fact an order.”
claims.changed: 4.33 says more: that all things are joint causes of all the things that come about. That is kept in the practice claim. 4.22 says that all things “feel with one another”, and 4.33 speaks of a “spinning together and winding together”; the claim says “bound to one another” for both. “Throughout” is the claim’s word for what 4.22 calls “an arranged order” and sets against a jumble.

support.quote: the universe as one living thing, having one substance and one soul
gives: The world is one thing
support.follows: The world is one living thing with one soul.

support.quote: all the things that come about, exist at once within the one and entire thing, the very thing we call the universe
gives: The world is one thing
support.follows: All the things that happen exist at once inside one whole thing, the thing we call the universe.

support.quote: or unity and order and providence
gives: The world is one thing
ordered throughout
support.note: The second of two cases. The first is under “said once”.
support.follows: The second possibility is unity, order and providence.

support.quote: Either an arranged order, or a stirred brew jumbled together. But in fact an order.
gives: ordered throughout
support.note: He names two cases and decides for the first.
support.follows: The whole is either an arranged order or a jumble, and in fact it is an order.

support.quote: and what the spinning together and winding together is like
gives: all things in it are bound to one another
support.follows: The things of the world are spun together and wound together.

support.quote: all things are, as they are, separated out and spread out, and feel with one another
gives: all things in it are bound to one another
support.follows: All things are distinct and spread out, and all of them feel with one another.

claims.t: What governs it is reason, and everything that happens comes from it. It has no cause to do evil, it is for community, and even what is harmful follows from something good.
claims.shared: 6.1 names “the reason that governs” the whole, and 5.24 “the mind of the whole”. 6.1, 6.33 and 7.44 all say that whatever happens comes from it. The last three points each rest on one passage.
claims.changed: 6.33 says “every kind of harm”; the claim no longer softens this to “what looks harmful”. 6.33 says “those revered and beautiful things”; the claim says “something good”. 5.24 says “mind” and does not say “governs”; the claim reads it with 6.1 as the reason that governs. 6.1 says that all things come about “in accordance with” that reason, 6.33 that they come from “that common ruling part”, and 7.44 that they follow from the impulse of “the nature of the whole”; the claim says “comes from it” for all three.

support.quote: the reason that governs it has in itself no cause for doing anything bad
gives: It has no cause to do evil
What governs it is reason
support.follows: The reason that governs the world has no motive to do evil.

support.quote: The mind of the whole is social.
gives: it is for community
What governs it is reason
support.note: The quote names the mind of the whole. That this mind puts things in order is said two sentences later in 5.24: “it has ranked things one below another, one beside another”.
support.follows: The whole has a mind, and that mind is social.

support.quote: And all things come about and are carried through in accordance with it.
gives: everything that happens comes from it
support.follows: Everything comes about and is carried through in accordance with the reason that governs.

support.quote: All things come from there: they have set out from that common ruling part, or they come as a consequence.
gives: everything that happens comes from it
support.follows: Everything comes from the common ruling part: it either sets out from it or follows as a consequence.

support.quote: The nature of the whole set out by impulse to make the universe. But now either everything that comes about comes about as a consequence
gives: everything that happens comes from it
support.note: The first of two cases. The second, in which even the most important things would be irrational, is under “said once”.
support.follows: In the first case, everything that happens now follows as a consequence of the impulse by which the nature of the whole set out to make the world.

support.quote: and every kind of harm, like a thorn, like mud, are by-products of those revered and beautiful things
gives: even what is harmful follows from something good
support.follows: Every kind of harm is a by-product of revered and beautiful things.

claims.role: The same thing rules in me
claims.t: What rules in me is of one kind with it. It moves itself, and it turns everything else in me to its use. What I find in myself I can expect in the whole.
claims.shared: 5.18 and 6.7 both name a part of me that rules. 4.22 and 6.23 both argue from what is in me to what is in the whole. Only 5.18 says the two are akin, a word that in the Greek means “of the same kind”.
claims.changed: 4.22 speaks of order in me and 6.23 of many things happening in me at once; the claim says “what I find in myself” for both. 5.18 says “the others”, which are the other things in me, so the claim says “everything else in me”. 5.18 says “akin”; the claim says “of one kind”, which is what the Greek word means.

support.quote: this is what is akin to that other
gives: of one kind with it
support.follows: What is supreme in me is akin to what is supreme in the world.

support.quote: For in your case too, this is what uses the others, and your life is governed by it.
gives: it turns everything else in me to its use
What rules in me
support.follows: In me too, what is supreme is what uses the other things, and my life is governed by it.

support.quote: The ruling part is what wakes itself and turns itself
gives: It moves itself
What rules in me
support.follows: The ruling part wakes itself and turns itself.

support.quote: Or can a kind of order exist in you, and disorder in the all?
gives: What I find in myself I can expect in the whole
support.note: A likeness used as an argument: from order in me to order in the whole.
support.follows: If a kind of order can exist in me, there cannot be disorder in the whole.

support.quote: Consider how many things come about at once in each of us in the same instant of time, things of the body and things of the soul together. And then you will not be surprised
gives: What I find in myself I can expect in the whole
support.follows: So much happens in me at one moment that I need not wonder at the world holding all things at once.

claims.t: I shall make a habit of asking what causes each thing: the power at work in it, considered apart from its matter, and the one source of all things.
claims.shared: Only 4.33 makes it constant: “To think constantly of”. 10.26 says “to look” and “to see”, with no word for a habit. 9.23 and 4.33 both name causes (“the quality of the cause”, “joint causes”), and 10.26 names “the power” after speaking of “another cause”. 6.33 and 4.33 point at the one origin: “the source of all things” and “one impulse”.

support.quote: To think constantly of
gives: I shall make a habit
support.follows: This is something to think of constantly.

support.quote: and to see the power just as we see the power that presses downward and the power that rises upward
gives: the power at work
support.follows: I should see the power in things just as I see the power that presses downward and the power that rises upward.

support.quote: Go to the quality of the cause
gives: what causes each thing
support.follows: I should go to the cause and ask what kind of cause it is.

support.quote: and how all things are joint causes of all the things that come about
gives: what causes each thing
support.follows: All things are joint causes of everything that happens.

support.quote: mark the cause off from the material and look at it
gives: considered apart from its matter
support.follows: I should mark a cause off from the material and look at the cause.

support.quote: but consider the source of all things
gives: the one source of all things
support.follows: I should consider the source of everything.

support.quote: and how it does all things by one impulse
gives: the one source of all things
support.follows: The world does all things by one impulse.

claims.t: Thinking of the world as governed makes me calm, and I can stand firm and trust what governs it.
claims.shared: 7.44 and 6.8 end on the same effect: “calmer” in one, “I stand firm, and I take heart” in the other. Only 6.8 adds reliance on what governs.
claims.changed: 7.44 says “Remembering this”; 6.8 puts it as a condition, “if it is the second”. 7.44 says “calmer” and 6.8 “I stand firm, and I take heart”; the claim says “calm” for both. The claim keeps the thought and the calm, which both have.

support.quote: Remembering this will make you calmer about many things.
gives: Thinking of the world as governed makes me calm
support.follows: Remembering this makes me calmer about many things.

support.quote: But if it is the second, I feel reverence, I stand firm, and I take heart, relying on the one that governs.
gives: Thinking of the world as governed makes me calm
I can stand firm and trust what governs it
support.follows: If the world is unity, order and providence, I feel reverence, I stand firm and I take heart, relying on what governs it.

single.label: An instruction
single.t: I shall honour what is supreme in the world, and in the same way what is supreme in myself.
single.quote: Of the things in the universe, honour what is supreme: this is what uses all things and directs all things. In the same way, of the things in you too, honour what is supreme
single.why: Only 5.18 says “honour”. It is the one place where the likeness becomes an instruction.
single.follows: I should honour what is supreme in the world, and likewise what is supreme in me.

single.label: A strong claim
single.t: Nothing is harmed by it.
single.quote: nothing is harmed by it
single.why: Only 6.1 goes this far. It is kept apart so that the claim on what governs the world does not rest on it.
single.follows: Nothing is harmed by the reason that governs the world.

single.label: The second of two cases
single.t: If things did not all follow as a consequence, even the most important things, the ones the ruling part of the world aims at in particular, would be without reason.
single.quote: or even the most important things, the ones at which the ruling part of the universe directs a particular impulse, are irrational
single.why: Only 7.44 speaks of a particular impulse of the world’s ruling part, and only as the second of two cases. It backs no words of the claim on what governs the world, so it stands apart.
single.follows: If not everything follows as a consequence, then even the most important things, the ones the ruling part of the universe aims at in particular, are irrational.

single.label: The other case
single.t: If the world were only confusion, why should I wish to stay in it?
single.quote: Now if it is the first, why do I even want to spend my time in a random compound and a jumble of that kind?
single.why: Only here does Marcus say how the ungoverned case would feel. Article 3 carries his calmer answer.
single.follows: If the world were mere confusion, there would be no reason to want to remain in it.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek instead of Casaubon. Passage numbers stay Casaubon’s. In modern editions 4.22 is 4.27, 4.33 is 4.40, 5.18 is 5.21, 5.24 is 5.30, 6.7 is 6.8, 6.8 is 6.9 and 6.10, 6.23 is 6.25, 6.33 is 6.36, 7.44 is 7.75 and 9.23 is 9.25; 6.1 and 10.26 are the same.
Reads four descriptions of the world as one claim, and four of what governs it as another.

Says “reason” for what Marcus names in several ways. What governs the world is “the reason that governs” in 6.1, “the mind of the whole” in 5.24 and a “ruling part” in 6.33 and 7.44. What governs me is “the ruling part” in 6.7 and “what is supreme” in me in 5.18; no passage of the section calls it reason. The second “reason” of the statement is the editor’s word.
Makes the likeness between the whole and myself the centre of the article. Only 5.18 says the two are akin; 4.22 and 6.23 argue from myself to the whole, so the statement says “alike” and no more.
Keeps “nothing is harmed by it” out of the fused claim, and keeps the second case of 7.44 apart as well.
Joins 7.44 and 6.8 on calm as a claim of its own, under “In action”.

Follows the Greek in 7.44. Casaubon has the world’s reason caring for “his reasonable and principal creatures”; the Greek says that in the second of two cases even the most important things are “irrational”. The earlier item on care for those who reason is withdrawn.

Follows the Greek where Casaubon added words. Claim 3 says “everything else in me” again, because 5.18 has “the others”, which are the other things in me. Claim 5 says “stand firm” where it said “be patient”. 10.26 no longer backs the habit in claim 4: its “thou must use to” is Casaubon’s.
articles.limit: All twelve passages are used. This is a belief about the universe and the least argued of the five. Only 5.18 says that what is supreme in me is akin to what is supreme in the world; the statement claims a likeness and no more. If you do not hold it, Articles 1 and 2 still stand on what human beings share, and Article 3 keeps its last claim.

statement.t: The reason that orders the world and the reason that guides me are alike.

parts.words: The reason that orders the world

statement.kind: A likeness between the whole and myself
statement.form: Claims 1 and 2 describe the world and claim 3 turns to me. 5.18 says that what is supreme in me is “akin” to what is supreme in the universe; the Greek word means “of the same kind”. 4.22 argues from the order in me to order in the whole. What both give is a likeness, so the statement says “alike”, and claim 3 keeps “of one kind” on 5.18 alone. “Reason” is the word of 6.1. 5.24 says “the mind of the whole”, 6.7 “the ruling part”, and 5.18 “what is supreme” in me; the statement says “reason” for all of them, and that naming is the editor’s.

empty.breaks: No passage in this section describes losing sight of this, or recovering it.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, four of the five claims gain a second author, the empty “When it breaks” gets its first item, “In action” says what worship of the governing power is enough, and “Why” gains a limit: its care may miss one person.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains what follows for worship: to imitate what orders the world, by being good, is enough.

items.quote: all that you behold, that which comprises both god and man, is one
gives: The world is one thing
items.follows: Everything there is, divine and human, is one.
items.context: Seneca’s short rule for how to treat other people; “all that you behold” is the universe, gods and men together, of which we are parts.

items.quote: the divine reason also is set in supreme command over all things, and is itself subject to none
gives: What governs it is reason
items.follows: Divine reason commands everything and answers to nothing.
items.context: Opening of a letter that ranks the parts of a person; the rational part rules there as “the divine reason” rules over all things.

items.quote: One who thinks that they are unwilling to do harm, is wrong; they cannot do harm.
gives: It has no cause to do evil
items.follows: The gods are not merely unwilling to do harm; they are unable to.
items.context: On the right idea of the gods, which worship needs; “they” are the gods, whom the next section calls supreme commanders in the universe.

items.quote: even this reason which we possess is the same, because it is derived from the divine reason
gives: of one kind with it
items.follows: The reason in us is the same as the divine reason, because it comes from it.
items.context: Same opening of the letter; “this reason which we possess” is the rational part of the human soul, set beside the divine reason.

items.quote: the latter is the only thing that is not referred back to another, but rather refers all things to itself
gives: it turns everything else in me to its use
items.follows: The rational part answers to nothing else in a person, and everything else is referred to it.
items.context: Same opening: body serves soul and the soul’s lower parts serve its primary part; “the latter” is the rational element of that part.

items.quote: the force which inheres in all the seeds of things, giving them the power to fashion each thing according to its kind
gives: the power at work
items.follows: Wisdom studies the force inside the seeds of things, which gives them the power to shape each thing.
items.context: A list of what wisdom studies, as against the crafts; “she” is wisdom going back to the beginnings of things, and “them” are the seeds.

items.quote: they all hinge on one alone, and that will be the creative cause
gives: the one source of all things
items.follows: All causes depend on one cause.
items.context: Seneca rejects Plato’s and Aristotle’s lists of causes; “they” are those listed causes, and the “one” is the maker, which he has just called Reason.

items.label: action
items.t: To worship what governs the world, it is enough to imitate it: to be a good man.
items.why: Marcus says to honour what is supreme in the world. Seneca says what counts as worship enough.

support.quote: Would you win over the gods? Then be a good man. Whoever imitates them, is worshipping them sufficiently.
support.follows: To win over the gods, be a good man; imitating them is worship enough.
support.context: On how the gods should be worshipped; “them” are the gods, just called supreme commanders in the universe who control all things.

items.label: breaks
items.t: It is weakness to struggle against the order of the universe and speak ill of it, and to want to reform the gods sooner than myself.
items.why: Marcus has no passage in this section on what failing looks like. Seneca describes it, at the close of a letter on accepting what happens.

support.quote: that man is a weakling and a degenerate who struggles and maligns the order of the universe and would rather reform the gods than reform himself
support.follows: It is a weak man who fights and slanders the order of the universe and would sooner reform the gods than himself.
support.context: Close of a letter on accepting what happens as Fate’s law; “that man” is whoever fights events instead of giving himself over to Fate.

items.label: why
items.t: What governs the world guards the human race, though it is sometimes unmindful of one person.
items.why: Marcus’s 7.44 speaks of a particular impulse of the world’s ruling part, and only as one of two cases; it does not say whom that impulse is for. Seneca says the gods guard humankind and may miss one person. The two do not disagree.

support.quote: acting as guardians of the human race, even though they are sometimes unmindful of the individual
support.follows: The gods guard humankind but are sometimes unmindful of one person.
support.context: On what a worshipper should know of the gods; “they” are the gods, who command the universe and, he adds next, neither give nor have evil.
